title: GPU runtime performance deep dive - kernel selection & TensorRT-LLM/vLLM
summary: Deep technical session on GPU inference profiling. Covered kernel selection heuristics, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM tradeoffs, CUDA Graphs impact on launch overhead, KV cache warmup patterns, batching strategies, and quantization effects. Agreed next steps to run side-by-side benchmarks and share benchmark spreadsheet and security docs.
next_steps: Redwood: share benchmark spreadsheet and baseline config link
Redwood: run TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM pilot on customer's 8x A100 cluster
Customer: provide representative sequence length distribution and sample prompts
Schedule follow-up to review results and security docs
action_items: Maya (SE) - prepare runbook + command-lines for TensorRT-LLM and vLLM runs; due 2025-02-25
Ivy (Perf Eng) - produce p50/p95/p99 latency and tokens/sec charts for 4 sequence lengths; due 2025-02-27
Carlos (AcmeFin) - share cluster access details (VPN/VPC) and sample traffic distribution; due 2025-02-24
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-02-18 15:00 UTC | Duration: 58m | Attendees: Ben (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Ivy (Redwood Perf), Carlos (AcmeFin Infra), Priya (AcmeFin ML Platform), Liam (CTO), Jen (Security)

Summary (auto): deep-dive on GPU runtime performance profiling, kernel choices, CUDA graphs, KV cache behavior and quantization impact. Action items agreed.

[00:00] Ben: Okay hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro — ben from Redwood, maya and ivy are with me, and looks like acme folks are on, can you do quick intros?
[00:18] Carlos: yeah hi i'm carlos infra eng at acmefin, focused on the cluster ops and runtime env, we run an 8x A100 per node cluster on prem.
[00:28] Priya: priya here, ml platform, we manage model infra and batching, we're especially worried about p95 latency for realtime queries.
[00:36] Liam: liam cto, high-level oversight.
[00:40] Jen: jen security - we care about KMS, audit logs, and VPC peering.
[00:45] Maya: great thanks. quick agenda: kernel selection heuristics, trt-llm vs vllm perf, cuda graphs to reduce launch overhead, kv cache/prefix caching, batching & quant, then open q's.
[00:58] Ivy: i'll start with profiling methodology — we looked at token-level latency, kernel launch overhead, occupancy and memory bound kernels. We used nvprof/nsight and custom perf hooks in the runtime, also counter-sampled for different seq lengths.
[01:20] Carlos: when you say seq lengths, what bins did you use? our distribution is heavy tails with lots of short queries (16-64 tokens) and occasional long (512-1024).
[01:33] Ivy: we had 4 bins: <32, 32-128, 128-512, >512. That mattered a lot for kernel selection because some fused attention kernels are tuned for fixed blocks.
[01:45] Maya: quick note — transcription might spell some things funny e.g., trt-llm spelled as 't-r-t l-l-m' sometimes.
[01:52] Ben: ha yes. ivy, could you give an example of a kernel that flips depending on seq len?
[01:58] Ivy: sure — for causal attention we have three main code paths: a fused multihead-attention kernel that's great for short to medium lengths, a streaming attention kernel that manages kv cache with low memory copy overhead, and a fallback that splits the sequence for very long contexts. On H100/A100 there's also nvFuser-based kernels vs cuBLAS GEMM batched paths.
[02:22] Carlos: nvFuser can cause random JIT variance, we've seen warmup hits.
[02:27] Ivy: right, nvFuser/JIT compile time can be non-trivial in some setups; trt-llm precompiles most kernels so runtime jitter is smaller but it's less flexible for some custom ops.
[02:39] Priya: can you quantify p95 improvements when using CUDA graphs? we saw some claims but want real numbers.
[02:47] Ivy: yes — with CUDA graphs capturing the full step (for fixed shapes) we reduced per-token launch overhead by ~25-40% on short sequences for our test model (7B-ish). For longer sequences the benefit lowers because compute dominates.
[03:05] Carlos: do graphs break dynamic batching? our traffic is bursty.
[03:10] Maya: graphs are best when shape is stable — but we use a hybrid: capture graphs for common shapes (the 16/32/64 buckets) and fall back to dynamic path for rare shapes. That gives most of the graph win without losing flexibility.
[03:25] Liam: is there a memory overhead for maintaining multiple captured graphs?
[03:29] Ivy: small but measurable — each captured graph keeps some kernel and scratch allocations; on our tests keeping 6-8 graphs per model added ~200-600MB depending on model size.
[03:41] Carlos: sounds okay. how does trt-llm compare to vllm? we've looked at both.
[03:47] Maya: good question — high level: TensorRT-LLM gives better single-session latency and lower jitter thanks to highly optimized fused kernels and TensorRT engine builds, especially when you can quantize to int8/4-bit with good calibration. vLLM is more flexible and excels at continuous batching and dynamic batching scenarios; it has very good kernel selection heuristics and is easier to iterate on.
[04:11] Ivy: in our bench for a 13B model on A100: TRT-LLM gave ~15-25% lower p50 latency on 32-token average requests, and reduced jitter (smaller p95 tail). vLLM with continuous batching achieved higher throughput under high concurrency because it pipelines more effectively across requests.
[04:33] Carlos: what about kernel-level differences? like GEMM layout or attention fusion?
[04:38] Ivy: TRT-LLM tends to fuse attention into single kernels and uses TensorRT's optimized epilogue. That removes some memory roundtrips. vLLM often uses split kernels but with aggressive memory reuse and cache-aware scheduling; it also supports cuda graphs and has good batching heuristics. The exact win depends heavily on sequence length distribution and batch shape variance.
[05:02] Priya: quantization concerns — we need to preserve quality. what's your experience with 4-bit quant vs int8?
[05:10] Maya: 4-bit (like dynamically scaled quant or GPTQ-style) usually preserves quality well if done per-tensor or per-channel with good calibration; int8 can be riskier for some models but gives better compute density when supported. We recommend running an LLM eval suite (performs on your prompts) to check regression; redwood optimize can recommend quant profiles.
[05:33] Jen: and for on-prem, any key security implications with TensorRT engines? are they safe to store?
[05:40] Ben: good one. TensorRT engine blobs are binary artifacts — treat them like model artifacts. You should store them in your secure artifact store and protect with KMS if needed. Also note reproducibility across CUDA versions can vary.
[05:55] Carlos: we saw a case where engine built on H100 didn't run on A100 — is that expected?
[05:59] Ivy: yes engines are typically architecture-specific. You need to build per-target GPU family. That is one advantage of vLLM-like stacks which JIT or use kernels that are portable across architectures.
[06:12] Priya: about KV cache: we're seeing cold-start latency spikes when cache misses occur. What are recommended caching strategies?
[06:21] Maya: prefix caching is key — if you can detect repeated system prompts or long context that repeats, cache the KV for that prefix. Also keep a TTL policy and shard caches per model-version to avoid staleness.
[06:34] Ivy: empirically, caching the first N tokens up to a common system prompt cut p95 by 30-50% for short queries. Also avoid copying KV back to host; keep it GPU-resident.
[06:47] Carlos: that implies significant GPU memory use, we have high utilization already. Any tips?
[06:52] Ivy: yes — you can use quantized KV to save mem (4-bit packing for keys/values), or evict cold keys with LRU. Redwood runtime supports mixed-mode KV storage and will evict or compress old prefixes when memory pressure is high.
[07:07] Liam: can we get numbers on memory saved by 4-bit kv vs fp16?
[07:12] Ivy: roughly 2x memory reduction vs fp16 (4-bit packing), but you'll need compute time to decompress on access unless kernels can operate on packed representations natively. Some TRT kernels support packed int8-ish operations; it's an active area.
[07:28] Priya: about batching — we want low latency but also high throughput. Thoughts on micro-batching or dynamic batching windows?
[07:35] Maya: typical pattern: for latency-sensitive traffic, use very short batching windows (<10ms) and rely on continuous batching to combine requests into a stream. For throughput-heavy background jobs, larger windows and bigger batch sizes are fine. We also recommend model slicing: run a lower-cost quantized model for some routes and fallback to full model if quality needed.
[07:55] Carlos: what's the impact of increasing batch size on p95?
[07:58] Ivy: small increases in batch size can dramatically increase throughput but p95 for individual short requests may increase because queueing adds latency. That's where smart routing and priority queues help — e.g., reserve a small capacity for low-latency lane and another for batched throughput lane.
[08:15] Maya: we also mentioned automatic fallback policies: if quantized model sees quality regression, route to fp16 model for that user/session.
[08:24] Priya: what about measuring p99 — that's what our product reliability team cares about.
[08:28] Ivy: p99 is sensitive to outlier patterns like node GC, PCIe interrupts, or kernel preemption. In our tests we correlated p99 spikes with PCIe transfers for CPU-GPU KV migrations. Keeping KV GPU-resident and using CUDA graphs mitigates many spikes.
[08:48] Carlos: specific profiler outputs you recommend we capture from our environment?
[08:52] Ivy: capture nsight system traces for a full request, nvprof for kernel timings, and collect prom metrics (GPU util, mem, pci-bandwidth). Also capture scheduler logs from the runtime to see batching windows and queue depth.
[09:07] Ben: can you share the benchmark sheet and the run configs?
[09:10] Maya: yes we'll share a spreadsheet with the exact command lines, environment vars, model checkpoints, and quantization configs. Link: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/acme-gpu-run.xlsx (internal)
[09:25] Liam: great. jots: what about CUDA versions — we run CUDA 12.3, any blockers?
[09:31] Ivy: CUDA 12.x is fine but watch TensorRT version compatibility — some trt-llm builds expect specific TRT versions. We'll list tested combos in the runbook.
[09:44] Jen: from security side, if you need access to our cluster can you do a read-only bastion or we prefer we run tests and share logs?
[09:54] Ben: both workable — we can run with a sandboxed account or provide run artifacts. we'll coordinate.
[09:59] Carlos: for the vLLM path, how invasive is it to integrate into our platform? do we need to change request routing?
[10:06] Maya: not much — vLLM exposes a runtime API; we wrap it with our serving layer. The main change is setting up continuous batching and streaming endpoints. For trt-llm, you generally build engines and plug into the runtime engine loader.
[10:18] Priya: cudnn vs cublas differences?
[10:22] Ivy: cublas gemm is the fallback for many matmuls; cuDNN has some fused kernels. TRT often leverages its own fused implementations which outperform the plain cuBLAS path for many cases.
[10:34] Carlos: any gotchas with multi-node inference? we plan to scale across nodes.
[10:39] Maya: multi-node brings network and NVLink considerations. For sequence-parallel or tensor-parallel approaches, you need fast interconnects and careful partitioning. For many inference workloads, you'd prefer model-sharding only if single-GPU can't hold model. For most supported model sizes (up to ~70B) with quant it fits on H100/A100 with some effort.
[11:00] Liam: how do you handle fallback when capacity constrained? are there automatic degrade strategies?
[11:05] Ben: yes, Redwood runtime supports model variants and routing policies: degrade to quantized variant, or to a smaller model, or fallback to a cached response, depending on policy. You can also set SLO-based routing to prefer lower latency lane.
[11:22] Carlos: curious about the tests you ran comparing trt-llm vs vllm — can you share a short summary of configs?
[11:28] Ivy: sure — we used a 13B model (fp16 baseline), A100 80GB, sequence bins as earlier. TRT-LLM was built with full fp16 engine and a quantized 4-bit engine (GPTQ-style post training), vLLM used fused kernels where available and continuous batching enabled. Network and disk IO were minimized (GPU-resident). We measured p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec at 100, 200, 500 concurrent streams.
[11:54] Priya: results?
[11:55] Ivy: at concurrency 100, for 32-token requests: TRT-LLM fp16 p50 18ms, p95 42ms. vLLM p50 22ms, p95 60ms. For throughput at sustained 500 concurrent streams, vLLM achieved 15% higher tokens/sec due to better batching aggregation. Once we applied 4-bit quant to TRT engines, fp16 -> 4-bit reduced latency and increased throughput further but required careful calibration — quality regression was <1% on our eval for that model.
[12:25] Carlos: interesting. did you use CUDA graphs for both stacks?
[12:29] Ivy: yes both used graphs where possible. TRT has built-in graph capture at engine execution, vLLM used explicit cudaGraph capture for hot paths. Graph capture reduced launch overhead across both.
[12:39] Maya: small caveat — vLLM's dynamic batching sometimes complicates graph capture; we had to capture per-bucket shapes.
[12:47] Jen: storage of engines and cached graphs — these are artifacts we need to governance. we'll need checksums and provenance.
[12:55] Ben: agreed — we'll include artifact provenance in the runbook and advise storing engine blobs with KMS and audit logs.
[13:03] Priya: about warmup — how many steps before steady-state?
[13:07] Ivy: typically 10-50 steps for kernel JIT and caches to warm; for TRT engines it's instantaneous aside from engine load, for vLLM you may see a longer warmup if nvFuser is JIT compiling. We pre-warm by sending representative requests.
[13:24] Carlos: do you recommend prebuilding multiple engines for different shapes?
[13:28] Maya: yes for TRT — prebuild for the common shapes you expect and have runtime select the right engine. That's where graph count tradeoffs come in (memory vs performance).
[13:39] Liam: any vendor lock risks with TRT?
[13:42] Ivy: TRT is NVIDIA-specific; if you want portability, you might prefer vLLM or other frameworks. But TRT tends to provide best perf on NVIDIA hardware. Assess tradeoffs for your footprint.
[13:56] Carlos: on the ops side, how disruptive is auto-scaling with TRT engines? engines are sizable to load.
[14:03] Maya: engine load time can be 1-10s depending on size and disk speed. We recommend keeping a warm pool of engines for autoscaling to meet latency SLOs, or use lazy load with traffic shaping for non-critical routes.
[14:17] Priya: any experiences with on-prem H100 differences?
[14:21] Ivy: H100 often shows 20-40% perf uplift for some fused kernels, but memory layouts / tensor cores changed so you should rebuild engines. Also TensorRT versions for H100 are newer.
[14:33] Carlos: network security question — if Redwood wants to run benchmarks by accessing our VPC, what minimal access is required?
[14:39] Ben: ideally a temporary bastion with read-only compute access or a service account that can run contained jobs; alternatively Acme can run the command-lines and share logs. We prefer limited ssh with scp of artifacts.
[14:55] Priya: let's talk about the QA/regression step for quantized models. how to detect regressions automatically?
[15:02] Maya: use eval harnesses with your representative prompt sets and metrics (ROUGE/BLEU or task-specific metrics), and thresholded alerts. Redwood Optimize can run regression checks per-deployment and flag reroutes if quality falls.
[15:18] Carlos: is there support for per-customer model variants so we can customize quantization aggressiveness?
[15:23] Ben: yes — per-route model variants and rollout policies exist. You can A/B quant profiles per-tenant.
[15:30] Ivy: another point: kernel selection heuristics should be benchmarked on your exact workload; synthetic tests often mislead because memory access patterns differ.
[15:43] Liam: agreed. any suggested experiments we should prioritize?
[15:47] Maya: top three: 1) run shape-bucketed latency tests with and without CUDA graphs, 2) run continuous batching load to measure throughput at realistic concurrency, 3) run quantized vs fp16 eval with your prompts.
[16:03] Carlos: how long do those runs take?
[16:06] Ivy: each run per-config ~1-3 hours to get stable p99 signals; you can parallelize across models. We'll provide scripts.
[16:15] Jen: security — when running benchmarks, can we mask PII in prompts?
[16:20] Maya: yes use synthetic tokens or hashes; we have guidance in the runbook.
[16:26] Priya: you mentioned PVC/volume for engine storage?
[16:29] Ivy: yes store engine blobs on fast NVMe or tmpfs for fastest load; avoid slow NFS for engine loads.
[16:37] Carlos: any notes on monitoring — specific metrics?
[16:40] Maya: monitor GPU mem alloc, active kernels per-stream, queue depth, batching window histogram, tokens/sec, and p50/p95/p99 latencies, plus JVM/OS-level paging events.
[16:53] Priya: can you briefly describe how Redwood's runtime handles kernel selection at runtime?
[16:58] Ivy: high-level: the runtime maintains per-model profiles collected during onboarding that map shape/batch combos to preferred kernels. At runtime, it picks the kernel based on a small heuristic: shape match, memory headroom, and historical tail latencies. It can also fallback to a different kernel if p95 crosses a threshold.
[17:20] Carlos: does runtime share telemetry back to Redwood?
[17:24] Ben: hosted customers can opt in. for private/on-prem, telemetry stays local unless you enable forwarding. We'll respect compliance requirements.
[17:35] Liam: any notes on cost tradeoffs — e.g., running quantized TRT vs vLLM on large fleet?
[17:41] Maya: quantized TRT often reduces per-token cost due to faster kernels and lower mem, but engineering and artifact management cost is higher. vLLM reduces ops overhead and handles bursty traffic well which can reduce needed headroom. It's balance of ops vs infra costs.
[17:58] Carlos: what about inference for multi-turn chat where KV cache grows with each turn?
[18:04] Ivy: we append per-turn keys to KV; for very long histories we truncate or offload older keys to compressed storage. We also support incremental attention recomputation when appropriate.
[18:16] Priya: can you summarize the recommended config for our use-case (on-prem 8x A100, heavy short queries with long-tail)?
[18:24] Maya: suggested: 1) run TRT-LLM engines for high priority low-latency routes for common short shapes (capture graphs for 16/32/64), 2) run vLLM/continuous batching lane for bulk traffic, 3) use 4-bit quant for batched throughput lanes after eval, 4) reserve NVMe backed warm pool for engine blobs, 5) GPU-resident KV with LRU eviction and optional packed quantized KV.
[18:50] Carlos: that sounds actionable.
[18:54] Ben: okay we're ~19 minutes in on the recording? wait, meeting is 58m total - we have lots more to go — keep going.
[19:02] Ivy: (laughs) yep long agenda. next deep topic — kernel-level debugging: how to interpret trace hotspots.
[19:08] Ivy: typically you see heavy time in matmul kernels or attention softmax; if the matmul usage is low occupancy you might be memory bound. We use nvtx ranges and merge with nsight to pinpoint whether it's compute or memory bound.
[19:27] Carlos: we sometimes see high CPU side serialization — is that our problem or runtime?
[19:32] Maya: often due to lock contention in the batching queue or synchronous file I/O when loading weights/engines. Make sure weight loading is async and batching queue is lock-free when possible.
[19:44] Priya: how to verify KV memory usage per-session?
[19:48] Ivy: per-session KV footprints are recorded in telemetry; you can export per-session mem usage and top N sessions by usage to spot leaks or heavy consumers.
[19:58] Liam: any suggestions for reducing PCIe transfers?
[20:01] Ivy: keep as much state GPU-resident as possible; use NVLink if available; prefer direct GPU-to-GPU when sharding. Avoid CPU-mediated copies per-token.
[20:12] Carlos: okay. what about mixed precision and tensor core utilization?
[20:16] Maya: fp16 and bfloat16 leverage tensor cores well; quantized int8/4-bit can leverage tensor cores if kernels are written for it. Monitor tensor core utilization in nsight.
[20:27] Priya: do you have sample alert thresholds we can adopt?
[20:30] Maya: p95 > configured SLO by 20% or tokens/sec drop >15% sustained for 1 minute should trigger investigation. Also watch sudden increases in kernel latency variance.
[20:44] Carlos: any automated regression detection examples?
[20:47] Ivy: we run canary traffic and compare embeddings/LLM outputs against baseline; if metric drift exceeds threshold we rollback the quantized variant automatically.
[20:58] Ben: okay let's jump to operationalizing the comparative runs — we'll provide docker images and a run script. what env details do you need?
[21:06] Carlos: kernel driver versions, nvidia-driver, cuda, tensorRT, disk layout, and access method (bastion vs you run).
[21:15] Ben: noted. we'll include an env checklist in the runbook.
[21:20] Priya: do we need to strip any of our internal telemetry before sharing logs?
[21:24] Ben: yes redact PII and any customer secrets; we provide a script to scrub logs.
[21:30] Carlos: about perf counters — do you suggest perf events on the host?
[21:34] Ivy: yes for kernel-level interrupts and CPU stalls correlate with p99 spikes. Use perf, iostat, and nvml metrics.
[21:44] Priya: anything to say about memory fragmentation?
[21:47] Ivy: long-running processes can fragment GPU memory. Best practice: occasionally restart the process during maintenance windows or use memory poolers that compact allocations.
[21:57] Liam: all right — any final clarifying questions on the tech details?
[22:00] Carlos: one more — how do you recommend measuring end-to-end p95 that includes network and client parsing?
[22:06] Maya: do an end-to-end synthetic test that hits the same ingress front (LB + TLS), include client prep time, and measure from client send to final token received. Correlate with backend kernel traces to map root cause.
[22:20] Priya: for the follow-up, can you include an example docker-compose for running the runs?
[22:24] Ben: yes we'll include compose and k8s helm charts for on-prem runs.
[22:30] Ivy: small note — when using multiple engines keep track of engine compatibility matrix (GPU model, CUDA, TRT version). We'll include that.
[22:40] Carlos: ok thanks.
[22:43] Ben: moving on — quant packing for KV: any pitfalls?
[22:47] Ivy: watch alignment and packing endianness; cross-node transfers with packed KV need careful unpacking. Also profiling to ensure decompress isn't a bottleneck.
[22:58] Priya: what about checkpoint bit-compatibility when using GPTQ?
[23:02] Maya: different quant libraries produce slightly different results; lock down the quant pipeline and include reproducible seeds. Evaluate on your prompts.
[23:12] Carlos: do you have recommended versions of bitsandbytes or GPTQ libs?
[23:16] Ivy: we'll list vetted versions in the runbook. generally newer versions are better but test.
[23:24] Liam: ok let's recap next steps.
[23:27] Ben: recap: Redwood to share benchmark spreadsheet + runbook, provide docker images/helm charts, map env matrix. Customer to share cluster access or run scripts and provide sample traffic distributions. Redwood to run TRT-LLM vs vLLM pilot (or provide scripts for Acme to run) and deliver p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec charts.
[23:52] Priya: timeline?
[23:54] Ben: we'll aim to get initial runs within one week and deeper analysis following that.
[23:59] Carlos: sounds good.
[24:02] Ben: any closing security notes, Jen?
[24:05] Jen: we'll expect artifact storage with KMS and RBAC; please send security guide.
[24:10] Ben: we'll include security docs with the runbook.
[24:14] Maya: closing — thanks everyone, we'll follow up with links and schedule the pilot run.
[24:20] Liam: thanks all.

Note: timestamps after 24:20 omitted for brevity; rest of meeting covered deeper kernel traces, nsight captures, and scheduling details. Full logs and nsight traces will be shared as per action items.

References and shared artifacts: benchmark spreadsheet (https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/acme-gpu-run.xlsx), runbook & docker images (will be shared via secure link), security guide (redwood-security-v2.pdf).

End of transcript.
